findings.finding: Insights: f(N) = smallest integer with three distinct divisors summing to N. For N≈M=3^{2025!}, any sum N=M+Δ must include divisor M, so N=M+3^a+3^b (Δ sum of two distinct powers of 3) ⇒ f(N)=M. Otherwise f(N)≫M. Compute k_i=⌊2025!·f(N)/M⌋: if f(N)=M ⇒ k_i=2025!; else k_i≈0. Identify which c give Δ as sum of two powers of 3. Sum k_i, divide by 2025! → S = (#valid c). p+q = (2025!·#valid c)+(2025!)/gcd → mod 99991. (Watch large factorial, reduce mod.)

Insights: f(n)=min LCM of two distinct divisors of n‑1.  
If S=n‑1 composite → let p=smallest divisor >2 of S; then f=S·(p‑1)/p.  
If S prime → f=2(S‑2).  

Compute S_i=M+c_i‑1 for the six c’s.  
Find p_i (smallest divisor >2) → f_i.  

g(c)=⌊2025!·f_i/M⌋/2025! ⇒ k_i=⌊2025!·f_i/M⌋.  
Sum K=∑k_i.  

Result p/q = K/2025! reduced; p+q = (K+2025!)/gcd(K,2025!).  

Pitfalls: exclude divisor 2 (gives equal numbers), handle S prime case, ensure p>2, treat large c=4M (S≈5M).

Insights: f(n)=min c (c’s proper divisors a≠b with a+b=n−c). For n≈M=3^{2025!}, optimal c≈α M with α∈[0.545,0.667]; f(M+c)/M≈α depends only on (M+c) mod 9. Since M≡0 (mod 9), α is determined by c mod 9. Compute α for residues 0‑8 using small‑M experiments (e.g., M=3⁵). Then g(c)=⌊2025!·α⌋/2025! (floor of 2025!·α). Sum six g’s, get rational p/q (denominator divides 2025!). Reduce, find p+q mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure α exact (as fraction with denominator 3^k), handle floor correctly; verify pattern holds for all large M (powers of 3).

Insights: f(N)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=N. For N≥30 the optimum has LCM = c (largest) ⇒ need L (c) and distinct proper divisors a,b of L with a+b=N−L. So f(N)=min L≥⌈N/2⌉ s.t. N−L∈{sum of two distinct proper divisors of L}.  

Maximizing (a+b)/L gives smallest L/N. Largest possible sum uses two biggest proper divisors L/p+L/q where p<q are smallest prime factors of L.  

If L divisible by 2&3 ⇒ (a+b)/L=5/6 ⇒ L/N=6/11 (requires N≡0 (mod 11)).  
Next best: L divisible by 2&5 ⇒ (a+b)/L=7/10 ⇒ L/N=10/17 (requires N≡0 (mod 17)).  
Then 2&7 ⇒ 9/14 ⇒ L/N=14/23 (N≡0 (mod 23)), etc.  

For huge N=M=3^{2025!} (≡ 1,3,4,5,9 mod 11,17,23,…), the smallest admissible ratio comes from the smallest pair of primes (p,q) with N≡0 (mod (p+q)). Compute N mod each candidate (11,17,23,…) to find first that divides N.  

Once L/N = p/(p+q) found, f(N)=L = (p/(p+q))·N.  

Then g(c)=⌊2025!·f(N)/M⌋/2025! = ⌊(p/(p+q))·(N/M)·2025!⌋/2025!. Since N=M+c, N/M=1+ c/M≈1 (c≪M). So g(c)≈p/(p+q) (fractional part negligible).  

Compute g for each c, sum fractions → p/q. Add p+q, mod 99991.  

Pitfalls: Small N (<30) need brute; ensure a,b distinct; verify N−L>0; handle c=4M (N=5M) where N/M=5. Use same ratio logic (N multiple of M). Use exact integer arithmetic for mod.

Insights: f(n)=min c with distinct proper divisors a,b|c, a+b=n−c. Since a≤c/2, b≤c/3 ⇒ a+b≤5c/6 ⇒ n≤11c/6 ⇒ c≥6n/11. If n≡0 (mod 11) then c=6n/11 works (c multiple of 6, a=c/2, b=c/3). Thus f(n)=6n/11 for all n≡0 (mod 11); this is the global minimum ratio. Use this to compute f(M+c) for given c (all ≡0 (mod 11)?) then g(c)=⌊2025!·f/M⌋/2025! = (6/11)·(M+c)/M truncated → (6/11)+(6c)/(11M) (tiny). Sum six terms → 6·6/11 = 36/11. Reduce p/q=36/11 ⇒ p+q=47. Answer: 47 mod 99991 = 47.

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) for a+b+c=n. Minimal ratios (lcm/sum) are record‑low for sums 9→2/3, 25→16/25, 47→30/47, 97→64/97, 167→110/167; 11 gives 6/11, 7 gives 4/7.  
M=3^K ⇒ M≡0 (mod 9) and ≡1 (mod s) for s coprime to 3.  
Check each n=M+c (c small) for smallest divisor S from the list; ratio = L/S.  
g(c)=ratio (c≠4M) and g(4M)=5·(2/3)=10/3.  
Sum = 2/3+10/3+16/25+30/47+64/97+110/167 = 125561848/19033825.  
(p+q) mod 99991 = 8687.  
Pitfalls: assume f uses 1,d,x; actually need full min‑lcm search; ensure S divides n; 2025! multiples make floor exact.
